name: Angelo Clareno
knownFor: A leader of the Franciscan Spirituals, the friars who wanted the Rule of Francis kept to the letter. He was jailed in Italy, fled with his brothers to Greece and was questioned at Avignon by Pope John XXII, and defended his brothers as no heretics. His commentary on the Rule and his letter of defense survive. Franz Ehrle judged him the most likely writer of the History of the Seven Tribulations.
dates: Paul Sabatier, editing the Mirror of Perfection, gives his life as about 1245 to 1337. Livarius Oliger, his 1912 editor, places his entry to the order about 1270, against older writers' 1260. Oliger and Ehrle date the hearing at Avignon to about 1317. He died in June 1337 at the hermitage of Santa Maria de Aspro, on the 15th by Oliger and Ehrle. The Bollandists, from a contemporary record of his miracles, give 14 June. The year is Ehrle's reckoning, from a note dated to the Friday after Pentecost, which was also the feast of Saint Anthony, 13 June. Daniel Papebroch, a Bollandist, had found the years in which that Friday fell on 13 June.
place: The March of Ancona, where Oliger says he came from, Cingoli or Fossombrone. Cilician Armenia, as a missionary. Greece, where the brothers lived about 1295 to 1305, first on a small island whose name is lost, which Ehrle identifies as Trixonia. Avignon, where he was questioned. Subiaco, where he lived after 1318. The hermitage of Santa Maria de Aspro in the Basilicata, where he died.
role: Franciscan friar, never a priest, by his answer to the pope in the History of the Seven Tribulations; leader of the Spirituals after Liberatus of Macerata; writer and translator

keyWorks.title: Expositio Regulae Fratrum Minorum (commentary on the Rule of the Friars Minor)
keyWorks.about: written for a brother Thomas, to set out what Francis meant in the Rule. Oliger, who first printed it in 1912, dates it between 1321 and 1323. He notes that the later letters are far harsher in judging men and things.

keyWorks.title: Letter of defense (Epistola excusatoria)
keyWorks.about: written to John XXII to win his release, printed in full by Franz Ehrle in 1885. He writes that his brothers are no heretics, unless it is heresy to keep humbly what Francis believed about his Rule.

keyWorks.title: History of the Seven Tribulations of the Order of Friars Minor
keyWorks.about: a chronicle of the trials of the friars who held to strict poverty. It names no author. Ehrle printed it in part in 1886 and argued for Angelo; Döllinger also printed an extract. It tells the hearing at Avignon.

traces: Matthaeus Rader, a Jesuit, introducing his own Latin John Climacus, calls Angelo the first of Climacus's translators, as far as he knows. Ambrose of Camaldoli, Rader adds, found that version obscure, word for word. Rader grants that Ambrose does not give Angelo's name, and says the description makes plain who is meant.

His letters survive in one Florence manuscript, the Book of Letters of blessed Angelo of Clarino. Oliger thinks Simon Fidati of Cascia probably gathered them, and Simon wrote that he did not want his memory to perish.
A congregation called the Clareni was placed under the Friars Minor in 1472. Oliger says it is not yet fully settled whether it came down from him.
remembered: Simon Fidati of Cascia mourned him in a lament, as an angel in name and more truly in deed.
Bartholomew of Pisa, a Franciscan, calls him a remarkable preacher. Luke Wadding, the Franciscan annalist of the 1620s, writes that he lived a most holy life in the order.
Oliger notes that the old Bollandists printed his acts and miracles under 15 June, though his cult was never approved by the church.
Paulinus of Venice, a Franciscan bishop hostile to the Spirituals, wrote that he called himself Angelo because he pretended to have angelic revelations.
Henry Charles Lea calls him "a man of the firmest and gentlest spirit".

uncertain: Who wrote the History of the Seven Tribulations. The work names no author. Franz Ehrle argued in 1886 and 1887 that Angelo was by far the most likely writer, and Conrad Eubel and Oliger follow him. Affò, an eighteenth-century writer, asked on what ground Wadding gave it to Angelo. Ehrle reports doubts from Richard, writing in 1884, and from Professor Felice Tocco.

When he was born, and where. Paul Sabatier gives about 1245, and no other witness gives a year. Oliger names Cingoli and Fossombrone, and thinks Fossombrone is more commonly and perhaps more rightly held.
When he joined the order. Ehrle placed it not long after 1260. Oliger rejects 1260, since Angelo would then have kept the Rule for seventy-seven years, and concludes about 1270.

When the Avignon hearing and the letter of defense took place. Ehrle dates the letter to the summer of 1317. Annibali da Latera, in his Supplement to the Franciscan Bullarium, after Wadding, put it at the end of 1318 or early 1319. Eubel has the leaders summoned at the end of 1316 or early 1317.

Whether the 1334 arrest order was aimed at him. The bull does not name the heretic who called himself head of the Fraticelli, and Eubel adds Angelo's name in brackets. A week later, a friar questioned by the inquisitor Simon of Spoleto named Angelo Clareno as the Fraticelli's general.

Whether a bull of 1331 was aimed at him. John XXII's bull of 23 November 1331 names a leader, Angelo of the Spoleto valley. Oliger says Raynaldus seems inclined to take him for Clareno and Felice Tocco holds that he was, while Eubel doubts it and Oliger finds it not clear.

When he died. Ehrle fixed 1337 from a note at the end of the list of his miracles. The note is dated to the Friday after Pentecost, which was the feast of Saint Anthony, 13 June. Papebroch had already found that in the first half of the fourteenth century this Friday fell on 13 June only in 1317, 1337 and 1348. Ehrle ruled out 1348 because Simon Fidati died early that year. Ehrle reads the list as naming 15 June. The Bollandists, from the same contemporary miracles by Robert of Mileto, give 14 June. Older writers they cite gave 1294 and a year the text prints as 12340.
